question: A survey conducted by the consumer magazine Oko-test1 in Germany recently found highly toxic substances (such as antimony, dimethylformamide, lead, cadmium, banned phthalates, naphthalene and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) to be present in many items of clothing from ‘fast fashion’ chainstores. Various types of clothing would seem to contain dangerous substances.

More specifically, research appears to have shown pairs of women’s sandals to contain levels of harmful chemicals well above the limits set by the EU’s REACH legislation. These tests have raised significant doubts as to the quality of products manufactured outside the EU and sold in ‘fast fashion’ chainstores and hence posing a substantial risk to the health and safety of European consumers. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of any potential breaches of REACH legislation by low-cost products manufactured outside Europe?

What additional measures will it take to check items of clothing from third countries entering the European market so as to safeguard EU citizens and consumers against potential exposure to harmful substances contained in clothing products?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2024) The Commission recognises the challenge of supervising and enforcing compliance with EU legislation on imported goods, including for low-cost products. A strict EU regulatory framework is in place to prevent certain hazardous substances in articles for consumers.

Textile products placed on the market, including imports, are subject to the Regulation concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of chemicals (REACH)1. Most substances found in the survey2 are already banned or restricted in textiles3 and others may follow should it be warranted. It is the responsibility of Member States to enforce EU legislation.

Projects by the Forum for Exchange of Information on Enforcement4 aim to increase compliance with the REACH and the Regulation on Classification, Labelling and Packaging5 (e.g. on textiles)6. EU regulations on general product safety7, on a Single Market for Digital Services8 and on market surveillance and compliance of products9 also aim to strengthen enforcement.

In addition, national authorities must notify measures taken against unsafe products, through the Safety Gate Rapid Alert System10. The proposed reform of the EU Customs Union11 would strengthen the capacity of customs and other authorities to enforce compliance with EU rules on imports, including for ecommerce imports.

Furthermore, under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation12, the Commission is currently assessing13 the introduction of specific information requirements on the presence and use of substances of concern in textile products placed on the EU market (including imports). Performance requirements could also be set to restrict the use of substances hindering circularity, complementing existing EU rules.
